q: What is Azure DNS?
opts: A hosting service for DNS zones that resolves names using Microsoft's global name servers
A domain registrar that sells domain names and renews them automatically each year
exp: Azure DNS hosts DNS zones — public zones for internet-facing domains and private zones for VNets — on Microsoft's global network of name servers, so you manage records with Azure tools. It doesn't sell domain names, load-balance traffic or provide VPN connections.

q: Which CLI command creates a public DNS zone for contoso.com?
opts: az network dns zone create -g RG1 -n contoso.com
az network zone add -g RG1 -n contoso.com --dns
exp: az network dns zone create -n contoso.com creates a public DNS zone in Azure DNS, and its output includes the name servers to set at your registrar. For a private zone use az network private-dns zone create. The other commands don't exist.

q: Which CLI command adds an A record 'www' → 20.1.2.3 in zone contoso.com?
opts: az network dns record-set a add-record -g RG1 -z contoso.com -n www -a 20.1.2.3
az network dns add-record -g RG1 --zone contoso.com --type A --name www --value 20.1.2.3
exp: az network dns record-set a add-record adds an A record to a zone: -z is the zone, -n is the record name (www) and -a is the IPv4 address. If the record set doesn't exist yet, Azure creates it. Each record type has its own subcommand, such as cname or mx.

q: Which record type maps a name to another name (an alias), for example www → contoso.azurewebsites.net?
exp: A CNAME record makes one name an alias of another, for example www.contoso.com → contoso.azurewebsites.net. An A record maps a name to an IPv4 address, MX handles mail and PTR does reverse lookups.

q: Which record type directs email for a domain to mail servers?
exp: MX (mail exchange) records list the mail servers that receive email for a domain, with a priority for each. TXT holds text such as SPF and verification values, SRV locates other services, and NS delegates the zone.

q: Can a CNAME record set contain more than one record?
opts: No — CNAME record sets can hold only one record
Yes — a CNAME record set can hold up to 20 records
exp: A CNAME record set can hold only one record, because a name can be an alias of only one other name. CNAMEs also can't exist at the zone apex. A, AAAA and TXT record sets can hold many records.

q: You need to delegate subdomain dev.contoso.com to a separate Azure DNS zone. What do you add in the parent zone contoso.com?
opts: An NS record set 'dev' with the child zone's name servers
A CNAME record 'dev' that points to the child zone's SOA
exp: To delegate dev.contoso.com to its own Azure DNS zone, create the child zone (dev.contoso.com) and add an NS record set named dev in the parent zone, listing the child zone's name servers. CNAME, A and TXT records don't delegate.

q: What's the effect of a lower TTL on a DNS record?
opts: Changes propagate faster, but query volume rises
Records are deleted sooner, so zones stay smaller
exp: TTL (time to live) is how long resolvers may cache a record. A lower TTL means caches expire sooner, so changes reach clients faster, but resolvers query your name servers more often. It doesn't make records private or delete them.

q: How do you prevent accidental deletion of a production DNS zone and its records?
opts: Apply a CanNotDelete resource lock on the zone
Assign an Azure Policy with the Audit effect to the zone
exp: A CanNotDelete resource lock on the DNS zone stops anyone deleting the zone (and with it every record) by accident. Record sets can also be protected individually. Azure Policy Audit only reports, TTL is about caching, and a private zone wouldn't serve public users.

q: Which RBAC role lets a user manage records in a DNS zone without changing other resources?
exp: DNS Zone Contributor lets a user manage DNS zones and their record sets, but not who has access to them and nothing else in the subscription. (Private DNS Zone Contributor is the equivalent for private zones.) Network Contributor covers all networking, Contributor covers everything, and Reader is view-only.

q: How can you check that delegation to Azure DNS works?
opts: Run nslookup -type=SOA contoso.com and confirm Azure name servers answer
Check the Azure Advisor reliability page for a delegation recommendation
Run IP flow verify against port 53 of the Azure name servers
exp: Query the domain from outside, for example nslookup -type=SOA contoso.com or nslookup -type=NS contoso.com. If Azure's name servers (ns1-xx.azure-dns.com and so on) answer, the delegation works. Ping tests hosts rather than zones, and Advisor and IP flow verify don't check DNS.

q: Which alias record target types does Azure DNS support?
opts: Public IPs, Traffic Manager, Front Door/CDN, and record sets in the same zone
Storage accounts, VMs, key vaults, SQL databases, and any external IP address
exp: Alias records can point at an Azure public IP address, a Traffic Manager profile, an Azure Front Door or CDN endpoint, or another record set in the same zone, and they update automatically when the target changes. They can't point at external IPs, storage accounts or load balancer backend pools.

q: Which CLI command links a private DNS zone to VNet1 with auto-registration?
opts: az network private-dns link vnet create -g RG1 -z contoso.local -n link1 -v VNet1 -e true
az network vnet update -g RG1 -n VNet1 --private-dns-zone contoso.local --register-vms true
exp: az network private-dns link vnet create links a private DNS zone (-z) to a VNet (-v), and -e true (registration enabled) turns on auto-registration of VM records. The other commands don't exist.

q: How many private DNS zones can a VNet be linked to with auto-registration enabled?
exp: A VNet can be linked to many private DNS zones for resolution, but only one of those links can have auto-registration enabled. Otherwise VMs would be registered in several zones.

q: VMs in VNet1 and VNet2 (peered) must resolve each other's names through private zone corp.local. What do you do?
exp: A private DNS zone only answers queries from VNets it's linked to, and peering doesn't share DNS. Link corp.local to both VNet1 and VNet2 (with auto-registration if you want VM records created automatically), and VMs in both can resolve each other. Azure-provided DNS alone works only within one VNet, and public zones would expose the names.

q: On-premises servers must resolve names in an Azure private DNS zone without deploying DNS VMs. Which service?
exp: Azure DNS Private Resolver is a managed service, so you don't need DNS VMs. Its inbound endpoint gets an IP in your VNet that on-premises DNS servers forward to, which lets them resolve names in Azure private DNS zones. Public zones, Traffic Manager and Bastion don't do this.

q: Azure VMs must resolve names in an on-premises domain (corp.contoso.com). Which Private Resolver components?
opts: An outbound endpoint plus a DNS forwarding ruleset linked to the VNet
An inbound endpoint plus a public DNS zone with the same domain name
exp: For Azure VMs to resolve an on-premises domain, deploy a Private Resolver outbound endpoint and a DNS forwarding ruleset (rule: corp.contoso.com → your on-premises DNS IPs), linked to the VNet. Inbound endpoints handle the opposite direction, from on-premises into Azure.

q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: Private DNS zones are resolvable from the internet
A private DNS zone can be linked to VNets in different regions
Auto-registration creates records for VMs' private IPs
A private zone name can match a public domain name (split-horizon)
exp: Private DNS zones are only resolvable from VNets linked to them, not from the internet. A zone can be linked to VNets in any region. Auto-registration creates records for VMs' private IPs. A private zone can have the same name as a public domain (split-horizon), giving internal and external answers.

q: What are the main components of Azure Load Balancer?
opts: Frontend IP, backend pool, health probe, load-balancing rules
Profile, endpoints, routing method, and endpoint monitor settings
exp: Azure Load Balancer is built from a frontend IP configuration (where traffic arrives), a backend pool (the VMs that receive it), health probes (which check the backends) and load-balancing rules (which tie the frontend, backend and probe together for a port). Listeners and URL maps belong to Application Gateway, profiles and endpoints to Traffic Manager, and gateways and connections to VPN.

q: Which CLI command creates a Standard public load balancer?
opts: az network lb create -g RG1 -n lb1 --sku Standard --public-ip-address pip1
az network loadbalancer add -g RG1 -n lb1 --tier Standard --frontend-ip pip1
exp: az network lb create creates a load balancer. --sku Standard sets the SKU, --public-ip-address attaches a Standard public IP as the frontend, and you name the frontend and backend pool. Add probes and rules afterwards. The other commands don't exist.

q: What are the default health probe settings commonly used for an HTTP probe?
opts: Interval 5 seconds, path such as /health on port 80
Interval 60 minutes, ICMP echo to the backend's port 80
exp: Health probes check backends every 5 seconds by default. An HTTP probe requests a path such as /health on a port such as 80 and expects a 200 OK. Probes can be TCP, HTTP or HTTPS; ICMP isn't supported, and a 60-minute interval would be far too slow.

q: An HTTP health probe on /health returns 302 (redirect). What's the probe result?
opts: Unhealthy — HTTP probes need a 200 status
Healthy — any status from 200 to 399 passes
exp: An HTTP or HTTPS probe treats only a 200 OK response as healthy. A 302 redirect, a 404 or anything else counts as a failure, so that instance stops getting new connections. Point the probe at a path that returns 200 without redirecting.

q: Which protocols does Azure Load Balancer support in load-balancing rules?
opts: TCP and UDP (or All with HA ports)
exp: Azure Load Balancer is a Layer 4 load balancer, so its rules handle TCP or UDP (or All, with HA ports on an internal load balancer). It doesn't understand HTTP or HTTPS, and ICMP can't be load-balanced.

q: Which resources can be in a Standard load balancer's backend pool?
opts: VMs or VMSS instances (by NIC or IP address) in a single VNet
VMs in any VNet worldwide, as long as the VNets are globally peered
exp: A Standard load balancer's backend pool can contain VMs or scale set instances (added by NIC, or by IP address) that are all in a single VNet. It can't span VNets around the world, and App Service apps and storage accounts can't be backends.

q: VMs behind a Standard internal load balancer have no outbound internet access. Why?
opts: Standard internal LBs don't provide outbound SNAT
The NSG default rules deny outbound traffic to internet
exp: An internal Standard load balancer only handles inbound traffic from inside the network. It gives backend VMs no outbound internet access (no SNAT). Add an explicit outbound method such as a NAT Gateway. NSGs allow outbound internet by default, so they aren't the cause.

q: What does the Floating IP (direct server return) option on a load-balancing rule do?
opts: Keeps the frontend IP as the destination in packets sent to the backend
Moves the frontend IP to the paired region when all backends are unhealthy
exp: Normally the load balancer delivers packets to a backend with the backend's own IP as the destination. Floating IP (direct server return) keeps the frontend IP as the destination instead, which clusters such as SQL Server Always On listeners need. It doesn't make IPs dynamic, move them between regions or add a WAF.

q: What's the default idle timeout for TCP flows on Azure Load Balancer, and can it change?
exp: Azure Load Balancer's TCP idle timeout defaults to 4 minutes and can be raised (up to 100 minutes on load-balancing rules). After that time with no traffic, the connection is dropped. You can also enable TCP reset so clients are told when an idle connection closes.

q: What's the purpose of an outbound rule on a public Standard load balancer?
opts: Explicitly configure outbound SNAT for backend VMs
Route traffic from backend VMs to on-premises networks
exp: An outbound rule on a public Standard load balancer sets up outbound SNAT explicitly: which public IPs backend VMs use for outbound internet traffic and how many SNAT ports each VM gets. Inbound RDP uses inbound NAT rules, routing to on-premises uses gateways, and TLS termination is a Layer 7 feature.

q: Which load balancer distributes traffic across regions at Layer 4 using a global frontend IP?
opts: Internal load balancer with global peering
exp: The cross-region (global) load balancer has a global anycast frontend IP and spreads Layer 4 traffic across regional Standard load balancers, failing over between regions. Internal load balancers are private to one region, Application Gateway is regional Layer 7, and NAT Gateway only handles outbound traffic.

q: Order the steps to load-balance web traffic across two VMs with a public Standard LB:
items: Create a load-balancing rule (TCP 80, frontend → backend pool, probe)
Create the LB with a Standard public IP frontend
Add the VMs' NICs to the backend pool and create a health probe
Allow port 80 in the VMs' NSGs
exp: Create the load balancer with its Standard public IP frontend first. Add the VMs' NICs to the backend pool and create a health probe. Then create the load-balancing rule linking frontend, pool and probe for TCP 80. Finally allow port 80 in the VMs' NSGs, because Standard is closed by default.

q: Which TWO conditions cause a Standard LB to send no traffic to a backend VM?
opts: The NSG doesn't allow the traffic
The VM has a Premium SSD
The VM is in an availability zone
exp: A backend VM gets no traffic if its health probe fails (the load balancer takes it out of rotation) or if an NSG doesn't allow the traffic (Standard SKU blocks it by default). The disk type and the VM's availability zone have no effect on load balancing.

q: The health probe shows all backends down, but the app works locally on the VMs. What should you check?
opts: That the probe port/path responds and the probe source isn't blocked
That the DNS TTL is low and the frontend IP has been propagated
exp: Health probes come from 168.63.129.16 (the AzureLoadBalancer service tag). Check that the app actually listens on the probe's port and path, and that neither the guest firewall nor an NSG blocks that source. Storage tier, DNS TTL and budgets don't affect probes.

q: A backend VM can't reach the load balancer's own frontend IP (hairpin), but external clients can. Why?
opts: A backend instance connecting to its own LB frontend isn't supported when the flow lands on itself
A DNS issue makes the frontend name resolve to the wrong address inside the VNet, so the flow is lost
exp: Azure Load Balancer doesn't support hairpinning: when a backend VM connects to its own load balancer's frontend IP and the flow is sent back to that same VM, it fails. External clients aren't affected. Call the service directly or use a different design, such as a separate internal frontend.

q: Which Load Balancer metric shows whether backend instances are passing health probes?
exp: The Health Probe Status metric (DipAvailability) shows whether each backend instance is passing its health probe. Data Path Availability shows whether the frontend itself is reachable, the SNAT count is about outbound connections, and byte count is throughput.

q: Intermittent outbound connection failures appear from VMs behind a load balancer under heavy load. Likely cause and fix?
opts: SNAT port exhaustion; use a NAT Gateway or allocate more outbound IPs/ports
DNS throttling; lower the record TTL or deploy a second custom DNS server
exp: Each VM gets a limited number of SNAT ports for outbound connections through the load balancer. Under heavy load they run out, and new outbound connections fail intermittently. A NAT Gateway (or more outbound IPs and allocated ports in outbound rules) provides far more SNAT capacity. DNS TTL, NSG priority and disks aren't related.

q: Which Azure Monitor experience gives a topology and metrics dashboard for a load balancer?
exp: Load Balancer Insights in Azure Monitor gives a topology view of the load balancer's frontends, backends and rules, plus ready-made metric dashboards for health and data path availability. VM insights is for VMs, Container insights is for containers, and Advisor gives recommendations.

q: Which Application Gateway feature routes requests for api.contoso.com and www.contoso.com to different backend pools?
exp: Multi-site listeners on Application Gateway route requests by host name (the Host header), so api.contoso.com and www.contoso.com go to different backend pools on the same gateway. Path-based routing splits by URL path instead. HA ports and inbound NAT belong to Azure Load Balancer.

q: Application Gateway needs which subnet setup?
opts: A dedicated subnet for the gateway
exp: Application Gateway must be deployed into its own dedicated subnet, which can't contain other resources (the name is up to you). GatewaySubnet is reserved for VPN and ExpressRoute gateways, and AzureBastionSubnet for Bastion.

q: Which Application Gateway feature protects apps from SQL injection and cross-site scripting?
opts: Web Application Firewall (WAF) with OWASP rule sets
DDoS network protection with adaptive tuning rules
exp: The Web Application Firewall on Application Gateway inspects HTTP requests against managed OWASP Core Rule Set rules and blocks attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting. NSGs work at Layer 4, DDoS protection handles traffic floods, and health probes check backends.

q: Which service load-balances globally by DNS (priority, weighted, performance, geographic routing)?
exp: Azure Traffic Manager balances traffic globally using DNS: it answers DNS queries with the best endpoint according to the routing method (priority, weighted, performance, geographic and others). Azure Load Balancer and Application Gateway are regional, and NAT Gateway is for outbound traffic.

q: A global web app needs edge TLS termination, caching, a WAF, and fast failover between regions at Layer 7. Which service?
exp: Azure Front Door is a global Layer 7 entry point at Microsoft's edge: it terminates TLS close to users, caches content, includes a web application firewall and fails over quickly between regions. Traffic Manager works only through DNS, and the internal load balancer and NAT Gateway are regional.

q: Internal non-HTTP traffic (TCP 1433) must be distributed across SQL VMs inside a VNet. Choose:
exp: An internal Standard load balancer works at Layer 4, so it can spread TCP 1433 across SQL VMs on a private frontend IP inside the VNet. Application Gateway and Front Door are for HTTP(S), and Traffic Manager is DNS-based and public.

q: Which combination gives zone-redundant Layer 4 load balancing for VMs spread across 3 zones?
opts: Standard LB with a zone-redundant frontend and backend VMs in zones 1, 2, 3
Basic LB with a zonal frontend and backend VMs in an availability set
exp: A Standard load balancer with a zone-redundant frontend keeps serving if a zone fails, and backend VMs spread across zones 1, 2 and 3 keep the app available. The Basic load balancer is retired and never supported zones, Traffic Manager doesn't load-balance within a region, and Application Gateway v1 is Layer 7 and has no zone support.

q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: A Standard LB can mix VMs from two different VNets in one backend pool
An inbound NAT rule can map a frontend port range to multiple VMs in a pool
A health probe can use HTTPS
A Basic public IP can be used with a Standard LB
exp: A Standard load balancer's backend pool must be in one VNet. Inbound NAT rules can map a frontend port range to multiple VMs in a pool. Health probes support HTTP, HTTPS and TCP. A Standard load balancer needs Standard public IPs — SKUs can't be mixed (and Basic public IPs are retired).

q: Which load balancer type inserts third-party NVAs transparently in the traffic path, chained to a Standard LB frontend?
exp: A gateway load balancer chains third-party network virtual appliances (such as firewalls) into the traffic path of a Standard load balancer's frontend, transparently ('bump in the wire'), so you can insert or scale NVAs without changing routes. The other options don't chain appliances.

q: An app needs TCP traffic on port 443 balanced to backend port 8443. Is that possible?
opts: Yes — load-balancing rules map a frontend port to a different backend port
No — the frontend and backend ports of a rule must match, except for UDP
exp: Each load-balancing rule has its own frontend port and backend port, so traffic arriving on 443 can be sent to 8443 on the VMs. This doesn't need Application Gateway or HA ports.

q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: Azure DNS supports DNSSEC signing for public zones
An alias record can point the apex at a Traffic Manager profile
You can import a zone file into Azure DNS with the CLI
Azure DNS public zones need a VNet link
exp: Azure DNS supports DNSSEC signing for public zones. An alias record can point the zone apex at a Traffic Manager profile. You can import a zone file with the CLI (az network dns zone import). Public zones are reached over the internet, so they don't need VNet links — only private zones do.

q: A VMSS behind a Standard LB should send each client to the same instance for 30 minutes. What do you use?
opts: Session persistence (Client IP) on the rule plus a suitable idle timeout
Floating IP enabled on the rule plus a 30-minute health probe interval
exp: Session persistence set to Client IP sends all traffic from one client IP to the same scale set instance. Pair it with a suitable idle timeout so connections aren't dropped during the session. Floating IP, HA ports and outbound rules don't keep a client on one instance.

ctx: Requirements: public HTTPS web app in 2 regions, failover between regions, URL path routing (/api to API servers), WAF protection, and an internal TCP service for the API servers' cache layer.
q: Which design best matches?
opts: Front Door (global L7, WAF) → regional Application Gateways (path routing) → internal Standard LB for the cache layer
Traffic Manager (global DNS) → regional NAT Gateways (path routing) → public Basic LB for the cache layer
exp: Front Door gives a global Layer 7 entry point with a web application firewall and fails over between the two regions. In each region, Application Gateway routes /api to the API servers by URL path. An internal Standard load balancer handles the TCP cache layer privately. A single Basic load balancer, Traffic Manager alone or a NAT Gateway can't meet all of these.

ctx: contoso.com is delegated to Azure DNS. The apex has an alias record pointing to pip-lb (Standard public IP of LB1). LB1 has a TCP 80 rule and a health probe on /health. NSG on the VMs allows port 80 from Internet.
q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: If pip-lb is replaced by a new IP resource, the alias record updates automatically
Clients can reach the app on http://contoso.com if at least one backend probe is healthy
A CNAME could have been used at the apex instead of the alias
If /health returns 500 on all VMs, traffic is still delivered
exp: An alias tracks the referenced resource's IP changes, but replacing the resource with a NEW one means updating the alias target; healthy backends serve traffic; CNAMEs can't be at the apex; all-down probes mean no delivery.
